narrative:
METHOD NOTE FIRST, because it bounds everything below. The session's WebSearch budget was exhausted (200/200) after my first two queries, and the network egress proxy then closed: nike.com, zalando.de, kickz.com, eur-lex.europa.eu, climatepartner.com, carbonfact.com, decathlon.co.uk, basketball-bund.de, euroleaguebasketball.net and li-ning-europe.eu all returned 403 CONNECT denials to both WebFetch and curl. I could not independently re-verify the developer's own external citations (EuroLeague attendance, DBB memberships, the Decathlon price, the Li-Ning European storefront), which were retrieved earlier in the session when egress was open. So two of my kill attempts are external and eight are internal - run against the 2.9MB corpus the developer did not fully mine. That turned out to be the productive direction: the sharpest counter-evidence against Continental was already sitting in this evidence base, unread.

WHAT SURVIVED. The regulatory trigger is real and on time. My first search found no delay, no omnibus carve-out and no postponement of the 27 September 2026 application date for Directive (EU) 2024/825; multiple independent legal and compliance sources confirm it applies to products already on the market with no transition period and fines to 4% of turnover in the relevant member state. The geographic hole is also real and independently reproduced - the cross-dataset auditor names Europe 'the single largest hole' at under 2% of surviving signals and never a primary market, and the audit's own assessment of the base confirms it. The recommendation to fund a European read and to run an EmpCo legal review of current hangtag and PDP language survives every attack I made on it, and the audit independently instructed the same thing.

WHAT DID NOT SURVIVE. Five things, and three of them are fatal to Continental as a product.

FIRST, THE REGULATORY MOAT INVERTS. My second search establishes the decisive fact the spec does not confront: the Green Claims Directive - the instrument that would have required pre-market substantiation and third-party verification - was WITHDRAWN in June 2025 over SME-burden concerns. What remains, EmpCo, amends the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive to PROHIBIT generic environmental claims and self-created sustainability labels. It is a prohibition regime, not a substantiation regime. There is therefore no rule anywhere in EU law requiring a competitor to publish a number; the cheapest compliant response to EmpCo is to delete the sentence. adidas deleting 'at least 70% recycled materials' from an EU hangtag costs adidas approximately nothing and leaves Nike's Continental Spec differentiating against silence rather than against a visibly worse competitor. You cannot build a moat out of a rule that every competitor satisfies by saying less. The spec's own what-would-need-to-be-true #3 concedes this as a risk; my finding is that it is not a risk, it is the base case, because the EU already chose the deletion-compatible instrument over the substantiation instrument and did so deliberately.

SECOND, THE PRODUCT IS ALREADY IN THE PORTFOLIO TWICE, AND THE SPEC DOES NOT DISCLOSE IT. I read the other seven developed opportunities. OPP-03 'Twenty Washes' (confidence 60) already specifies 'a published 20-home-launder dimensional-stability and seam-strength standard (AATCC 135 / ISO 6330 at 1, 5, 10 and 20 cycles), printed on the hangtag with the test date'; already specifies bartacked pocket mouths and hem stress points; already states 'Durability as the lead claim in place of recycled content, with recycled percentage demoted to a compliance line' with the explicit rationale 'Meets the EU Empowering Consumers Directive from 27 September 2026'; is already 70/30 wholesale-weighted; and already names UK, Germany and France as its second lead-market tier. OPP-02 'Found Outdoors' (confidence 62) already owns the UPF/abrasion/outdoor claim and already established that the DNA UV Woven FN2659 exists. Continental's durability spec, its claims architecture, its EmpCo rationale, its channel logic and its UPF claim are all pre-existing in two higher-confidence opportunities aimed at the same regulation and, in OPP-03's case, at the same European markets. Strip those out and Continental's incremental product content is: a franchise name, a European colour palette, a jacquard waistband, and a EUR ladder the spec itself calls an analyst estimate. That is not an opportunity; that is a regional expression of OPP-03.

THIRD, THE PRICE IS PROBABLY A DE-RATING, NOT A MID-CORE RUNG - AND THE PROOF WAS IN THE BASE. The spec states there is no European price observation and anchors EUR 45 at 'roughly 1.5x' a EUR 29.95 team stock short. Searching the corpus for GBP figures, I found two European price observations the developer missed, both inside signals it cites or that survived: A01-S3's evidence chain carries a Trustpilot complaint that a GBP 50 pair of Nike shorts 'felt like a GBP 10 pair', and A01-S9 carries a second Trustpilot item, explicitly geography-tagged 'United Kingdom', about a parent unable to return GBP 45 Nike shorts bought for a son's birthday. GBP 45-50 is roughly EUR 52-58. If Nike's live European consumer-facing price for basketball shorts is already at or above EUR 52, then Continental at EUR 45 is not a new mid-core rung above a EUR 29.95 entry short - it is priced BELOW Nike's existing European core, and it trades the existing DNA business down rather than adding a rung. The entire price rationale is built on the wrong anchor.

FOURTH, THE PREMISE 'NO EUROPEAN CONSUMER VOICE EXISTS' IS FALSE, AND WHAT EXISTS IS HOSTILE. Those same two Trustpilot items are European consumer voice, in this base, about this category, at this price. The spec asserts three separate times that not one European consumer signal exists. It does, and both instances are negative: one is a value-perception complaint at exactly the proposed price band, the other a service complaint. That does not merely correct a sentence - it inverts the emotional framing of the brief. Continental is pitched as planting a flag in virgin territory; the only European consumer evidence in the base says Nike shorts at GBP 45-50 already feel overpriced to a European buyer.

FIFTH, THE FLAGSHIP UNOWNED CLAIM MAY NOT BE TESTABLE AS SPECIFIED. The spec's one genuinely differentiated claim is UPF 'to EN 13758-2 stated both dry AND at saturation'. EN 13758-2 is a garment classification standard and, to my knowledge - I could not verify this against the standard text because eur-lex and the standards bodies were egress-blocked, so treat it as a HYPOTHESIS requiring a materials-lab answer, not a fact - neither EN 13758-1/-2 nor AS/NZS 4399 specifies a wet-state test method. If that is right, the product's only unowned claim cannot be stated against a named European standard, which is the one thing the entire Continental Spec architecture requires of every claim on the panel. The claim would have to be published against a Nike-authored method - which is precisely the self-created-standard posture the spec says EmpCo makes unusable.

WHAT I COULD NOT KILL. The decision. Not the garment - the decision. Commissioning a European read and running the EmpCo hangtag review before 27 September 2026 is correct, cheap, dated, and required whether or not a single Continental short is ever cut. The audit independently reached the same instruction. I attacked it four ways (it is redundant with OPP-03's Europe tier; the read is not actually cheap; the yield will be thin; the deadline is three weeks away so the legal work is already too late to be strategic) and it held each time, with one qualification: the marketplace specialist's own narrative records that it ran a 'Europe/Decathlon' search and got almost nothing back, so the desk-research yield on Europe is demonstrably poor and the read will have to be paid-for primary and syndicated panel work, not a literature scan. It is still worth doing. It is just not free.

VERDICT. Continental survives as a research gate and a legal workstream. It does not survive as a product spec, a franchise, a price position or an SS28 line slot, and it should not be ranked against OPP-02 and OPP-03 as though it were one - it is a lower-evidence regional restatement of them wearing a new name. My recommendation to the Consumer Council: strip the garment, fund the gate, fold the European tier into OPP-03, and re-open a European product brief only if the read comes back positive on full-price sell-through above EUR 35. The spec's own best line is the right one, and it argues for exactly this: 'The cheapest way this opportunity can be right is if the read kills it early.' My attack says the read should be commissioned and the garment should be killed now, at no cost, without waiting.

kill_attempts.angle: Timing / regulatory trigger - is EmpCo actually landing on 27 September 2026, or will it slip like so much EU sustainability law?
kill_attempts.argument: The entire why-now rests on one dated regulatory event. EU sustainability legislation has been repeatedly delayed and simplified through the 2025-26 Omnibus packages; if EmpCo slips or is carved back, Continental has no timing case at all and becomes a Europe-flavoured recolour with a 34-confidence market thesis behind it.
kill_attempts.evidence: WebSearch (2026-09-03) across EU legal and compliance sources (Heuking, Boehmert, ClimatePartner, Sustenuto, Net Zero Compare, EcoClaim) found no delay, no omnibus provision and no postponement: member states were required to transpose by 26 March 2026 and the rules apply from 27 September 2026 with no transition period, including to products already on the market, with fines up to 4% of annual turnover in the relevant member state. Corroborated in-base as skeptic counter-evidence attached to A03-S5. The one qualifier found: many member states missed the March 2026 transposition deadline, so day-one national enforcement will be patchy.

kill_attempts.angle: Differentiation - does EmpCo actually create a competitive asymmetry Nike can own, or does every competitor comply for free?
kill_attempts.argument: The spec's core proposition is that EmpCo converts a compliance cost into a moat because competitors 'must either substantiate or delete'. That is only a moat if deleting is expensive or visibly worse. It is neither. EmpCo is a prohibition regime layered onto the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive; silence is always compliant and costs a competitor one line of hangtag copy.
kill_attempts.evidence: WebSearch (2026-09-03): the Green Claims Directive - the instrument that would have required pre-market verification and third-party substantiation - was WITHDRAWN in June 2025 over SME-burden concerns. EmpCo, what remains, amends the UCPD to prohibit generic environmental claims and sustainability labels not based on independent certification. Nothing in it obliges any brand to publish a substantiated figure. In-base, A03-S5's own implication is 'Do not spend innovation budget or hangtag real estate on recycled percentage as a lead claim', and the cross-dataset audit's resolution of the same contradiction is that percentage-on-a-hangtag is commoditised. Further, the spec's own what_we_still_dont_know #8 concedes EmpCo may govern only environmental claims - in which case the UPF, Martindale and shrinkage numbers Continental actually leads with get no regulatory asymmetry whatsoever, and the only claim EmpCo does touch is the recycled figure the spec deliberately footnotes.

kill_attempts.angle: Is it really NEW? - internal duplication against the rest of this same portfolio
kill_attempts.argument: Before asking whether a competitor already sells this, ask whether this programme already proposed it. Continental's two product pillars are a published wash-durability spec and a certified UPF claim. Both are the central proposition of other, higher-confidence opportunities in the same portfolio, aimed at the same regulation.

And /tmp/.../dev-OPP-02.json (confidence 62) owns the outdoor/UV claim on the live DNA UV Woven FN2659. Continental discloses neither overlap anywhere in its spec, contradictory_evidence or what_would_need_to_be_true.

kill_attempts.angle: Price - is EUR 45 a defensible mid-core rung, and is the anchor right?
kill_attempts.argument: The spec positions EUR 45 as roughly 1.5x Nike's 'visible European position' of a EUR 29.95 team stock short and says no other European price observation exists. If Nike's real European consumer price for basketball shorts is materially higher, EUR 45 is not a new rung above the entry - it is below the existing core, and Continental cannibalises full-price DNA business rather than adding to it.

kill_attempts.angle: The founding premise - is Europe really a total consumer void in this base?
kill_attempts.argument: Continental's emotional and strategic force comes from the claim, asserted three separate times, that 'not one consumer signal in this entire base has a European consumer as its subject' and 'no European consumer voice exists anywhere in this base'. If that is wrong, the brief's framing of virgin territory is wrong, and the developer's search of its own corpus was not thorough.
kill_attempts.evidence: The two Trustpilot items above are European consumer voice about Nike shorts, in this base, one of them explicitly geography-tagged 'United Kingdom' in surviving.json. Separately, the marketplace specialist's own research narrative in surviving.json records that it ran a 'Europe/Decathlon' search among its 15 queries - so Europe was in fact searched by at least one specialist and returned little, which is a materially different diagnosis from 'nobody looked'. kill_attempts.angle: Consumer need - is there any evidence anywhere that a published claims panel sells a basketball short?
kill_attempts.argument: Continental's entire reason to exist at EUR 45 is 'The Continental Spec'. The spec concedes no conjoint and no stated-preference evidence exists. Beyond the base, transparency-led and eco-claim-led apparel propositions have a poor commercial record.
kill_attempts.evidence: In-base: A03-S5 records that 'none of the retrieved consumer feedback mentions it as a purchase reason', and the cross-dataset audit correctly invalidates that inference as correlation-as-causation on a tiny biased sample - which leaves the base silent in both directions, not supportive. The base contains zero evidence that a claim drives a shorts purchase in any market. Outside the base I would normally cite the commercial trajectories of transparency-led apparel propositions (Everlane's Radical Transparency, Allbirds' per-product carbon labelling and its subsequent retreat from sustainability-led messaging) as analyst knowledge - but I must flag that egress was closed and I could NOT verify those in this session, so they are unverified background, not evidence. Net: the differentiator is untested on demand in this base and, to my knowledge, has an unpromising precedent record elsewhere.

kill_attempts.angle: Execution feasibility - can the one genuinely unowned claim actually be tested and published?
kill_attempts.argument: The spec identifies the wet-state UPF figure as 'the genuinely unowned claim' and requires every Continental Spec claim to be stated against a named European standard. If no standard method exists for wet-state UPF, the flagship claim cannot satisfy the architecture's own rule.
kill_attempts.evidence: HYPOTHESIS, not a fact - I could not reach eur-lex or standards texts (egress 403). To my knowledge EN 13758-1/-2 and AS/NZS 4399 specify dry-state UV transmission testing and garment classification, and no accredited European method covers UPF at saturation. If correct, the wet figure could only be published against a Nike-authored protocol, which is the self-created-standard posture the spec says EmpCo makes unusable, and which would also be the weakest possible legal footing for a published claim in 27 jurisdictions. A06-S7's counter-evidence separately establishes that the dry UPF 40-50+ claim is nearly free on polyester and is therefore not a differentiator on its own - so if the wet claim is not publishable, the UV pillar collapses entirely to a certificate on a commodity property. Requires a one-week materials-lab answer to confirm or clear.

kill_attempts.angle: Market size and the need's scale
kill_attempts.argument: Even granting European demand growth, is the prize big enough to justify a Europe-created franchise, a regional claims architecture and a markdown-governance commitment?
kill_attempts.evidence: A02-S1 puts European basketball gear at 4.9% CAGR (Grand View, 2025-2030), explicitly the slowest region named - and the audit demolishes that whole family of numbers as one Technavio report in four vintages surrounded by SEO resellers disagreeing by roughly 2x, so it is a bad number pointing the wrong way rather than a good number pointing the right way. A04-S3 supplies the absolute-size warning: Under Armour's entire global basketball business including Curry Brand is guided at USD 100-120M, roughly 2% of its revenue, and adidas basketball fell 21% in Q2 2026. kill_attempts.angle: Geographic generalisation - is the market tiering built on market size or on data availability?
kill_attempts.argument: The spec's Tier 1 is Germany, Spain, France, Italy and its Tier 3 'specialty-only test' is the UK. But the largest European participation number anywhere in this evidence base is English.
kill_attempts.evidence: The cross-dataset audit records Sport England Active Lives Children and Young People 2024-25 at nearly 1.1 million weekly under-16 basketball players in England (741,600 boys, 328,800 girls) - against Germany's DBB figure of 288,444 total federation memberships, which the spec makes its 'registry-grade lead'. These are not like-for-like metrics (weekly participation versus club registration), which is exactly the point: the spec ranks Germany first because a positive registry number happened to be findable there, and demotes England to Tier 3 despite it carrying the base's largest participation figure - a figure whose only fault is that its direction is -1%. Selecting lead markets on the sign of the one number you found is data-availability bias, not market prioritisation. Note the spec does flag the England provenance issue honestly (it sits under rejected signal A06-S10 and is carried by the audit under A02-S1).

kill_attempts.angle: Nike's right to win and cannibalisation of the existing European business
kill_attempts.argument: Continental requires EMEA creation authority Nike has never demonstrated in this evidence base, a governed EUR 35 markdown floor in the region with Nike's worst measured promotional pressure, and it lands a new EUR 45 franchise on top of an existing European DNA/Icon assortment nobody in seven files audited.
kill_attempts.evidence: A04-S4 (VERIFIED) records EMEA revenue -6% with Nike Digital -24% on heightened inventory and elevated promotions, and the CFO expecting marketplace conditions not to improve through at least H1 FY2027. A03-S9 (VERIFIED, FY2026 10-K) shows apparel units +1% with ASP growth from mix, already eroded by discounts - Nike is not currently demonstrating the pricing discipline the EUR 35 floor requires. The audit's evidence_base_quality section states flatly that 'there is no first-party Nike commercial data anywhere in the base... no sell-through, no unit mix by inseam, no markdown rate by SKU' and that 'not one price, spec or review claim in the entire base was confirmed against a retrieved product page'. The spec's own what_would_need_to_be_true #7 concedes Nike's existing EMEA basketball assortment has never been audited - which means the portfolio's single most common failure mode (three of seven files proposed products Nike already ships) is unruled-out here, and with a GBP 45-50 European price observation now in evidence, the likelihood that Continental overlaps live European product is higher than the spec assumes.

kill_attempts.angle: The research gate itself - is the one thing the spec really asks for cheap and correct?
kill_attempts.argument: Attack the surviving core directly: the gate is redundant with OPP-03's UK/Germany/France tier, the read is not cheap, its desk yield will be thin, and the EmpCo deadline is three weeks away so the legal work is reactive rather than strategic.
kill_attempts.evidence: Each of those lands partially and none is fatal. The audit independently instructed 'Before the portfolio is ranked, commission a minimum viable read on Europe (EuroLeague/Basketball England/DBB participation plus KICKZ and Zalando sell-through)' - so the instruction originates outside this spec and is not self-serving. The EmpCo legal read is required regardless of Continental, which makes its cost sunk against compliance rather than against this opportunity. The cost objection does land: the marketplace specialist's own narrative shows a Europe search was already run with almost no yield, so a real read needs paid retail panel and primary consumer work, not desk research - the spec's implied cheapness is overstated. And the redundancy objection lands: the read should be commissioned for the portfolio and for OPP-03's European tier, not as the first deliverable of a franchise called Continental.

strongest_counterargument: "You are proposing to differentiate on a regulation that every competitor can satisfy by deleting one sentence - and the product you want to build, we already have twice." That is the sentence that ends the meeting, and it has two halves a PLM cannot answer in the room. First: the EU deliberately withdrew the Green Claims Directive, the instrument that would have forced substantiation, and kept EmpCo, which only forbids unsubstantiated claims. Compliance by silence is free and universal. Nike will spend a franchise, a claims architecture, a legal review across 27 jurisdictions and a markdown-governance commitment to be loud in a category where being quiet is now the cheapest compliant posture - and the base contains no evidence, in any market, that a published claim sells a basketball short. Second: OPP-03 'Twenty Washes' already publishes the 20-wash ISO 6330 standard on the hangtag, already demotes recycled content to a compliance line explicitly citing the 27 September 2026 EmpCo date, and already names UK/Germany/France as lead markets - at confidence 60 on Nike's largest existing unit pool. OPP-02 already owns the UV claim on a short Nike currently ships. Continental asks for a new EUR 45 European franchise to deliver capabilities two better-evidenced opportunities already deliver, in the region with Nike's worst measured promotional pressure, against a price anchor that the base's own UK evidence (GBP 45-50) suggests is set below Nike's existing European core rather than above its entry rung. The honest board response is: fund the European read, put it against OPP-03's European tier, and do not open a franchise slot for it.
adjustment_rationale:
Down from 34 to 24. The developer was unusually honest - it disclosed the unfalsifiability, the missing price pages, the Sport England contradiction, the killed half of A03-S7, and the un-audited EMEA assortment. I am not marking it down for concealment. I am marking it down for three things it did not find, each of which removes load-bearing structure.

(1) THE MOAT INVERTS, -6. The spec treats EmpCo as an asymmetry generator and lists 'enforcement genuinely bites competitor claim language' as a risk to be tested. It is not a risk; it is the base case. The EU withdrew the substantiation instrument (Green Claims, June 2025) and kept the prohibition instrument (EmpCo). Under a prohibition regime, silence is compliant and free, so the regulation produces a floor rather than a moat. The one claim EmpCo genuinely touches is the recycled percentage - which the spec, correctly following A03-S5 and the audit, chooses to footnote. The regulation and the differentiator point at different things.

(2) PORTFOLIO DUPLICATION, -5. OPP-03 (60) and OPP-02 (62) already carry the published wash-durability standard, the EmpCo-driven claims demotion, the wholesale-first channel logic, the UV claim, and UK/Germany/France as markets. Continental's undisclosed incremental content is a name, a palette, a jacquard waistband and an admittedly unfounded EUR ladder. For a portfolio ranking, a duplicate at lower confidence should rank below its originals, not beside them.

(3) THE PRICE ANCHOR IS INVERTED AND THE VOID IS OVERSTATED, -3. The base does contain European price and consumer observations - GBP 45-50, both negative, one explicitly geography-tagged United Kingdom. If Nike's live European price is EUR 52-58, EUR 45 is a de-rating of existing business rather than a new mid-core rung, and the 'roughly 1.5x the KICKZ stock short' arithmetic is built on the wrong comparator. Separately, 'no European consumer voice exists' is stated three times and is false against the developer's own corpus.

Smaller deductions: the wet-state UPF claim may have no standard method (-1, held small because it is my hypothesis and unverified); the research gate is not as cheap as implied, since Europe was already searched once with near-zero yield (-1); and the Tier 1/Tier 3 market ranking is driven by which sign of number was findable rather than by market size (-1).

What holds it at 24 rather than in the teens: the regulatory deadline verified clean with no delay, which is more than most why-now claims in this portfolio survive; the geographic hole is real and independently reproduced by the auditor; the EmpCo legal read is required regardless and is genuinely time-critical at three weeks out; and the underlying decision - fund a European read before ranking the portfolio - is correct and survived four separate attacks. A number below 20 would imply the ask itself is wrong. It is not. The garment wrapped around it is.

validation_plan.question: What does Nike actually sell as basketball shorts in EMEA today - SKU count, inseam mix, EUR/GBP price ladder by market, full-price sell-through and markdown rate by franchise - and does a European expression already occupy this space?
validation_plan.method: Internal pull, no external research required. EMEA merchandising and demand-planning extract for the basketball shorts class, FY24-FY26: SKU list by inseam and franchise, list price by market, realised ASP, full-price sell-through %, markdown rate and weeks-of-supply, split Nike Direct vs wholesale. Pair with a same-day rack walk of three KICKZ doors, one JD Sports Europe and one Intersport/SportScheck to photograph the live European price ladder. This must run FIRST and gates everything else - it is the cheapest and largest unknown in the brief, and it directly tests whether EUR 45 is above or below Nike's live European core.
validation_plan.who: Nike EMEA Merchandising + Demand Planning, with one Category Insights analyst; rack walk by the EMEA basketball merchant team
validation_plan.cost_time: Internal data pull 3-5 working days, effectively zero incremental cost. Rack walk 1 day, under EUR 2,000. Total: one week.

validation_plan.question: Does EmpCo create any competitive asymmetry Nike can own - specifically, does it reach performance and durability claims or only environmental ones, and what is the liability of publishing a numeric wash-shrinkage and Martindale figure on a hangtag across 27 member states plus the UK?
validation_plan.method: Formal legal opinion from Nike EMEA Legal with outside EU consumer-law counsel, covering: (a) EmpCo's scope over non-environmental claims after the Green Claims Directive withdrawal; (b) whether a published test figure constitutes a commercial guarantee of durability with warranty consequences; (c) US and Greater China disclosure spillover; (d) national transposition status by market as of the opinion date. Run in parallel: the EmpCo compliance review of Nike's CURRENT basketball shorts hangtag and PDP language, which is required before 27 September 2026 whether or not Continental proceeds. Do this second only because it needs no market data - in practice start it the same day.
validation_plan.who: Nike EMEA Legal + external EU consumer-law counsel; Nike Global Apparel Compliance for the hangtag review
validation_plan.cost_time: Legal opinion 3-4 weeks, EUR 40-70k. Hangtag/PDP compliance review 2-3 weeks, internal plus roughly EUR 25k - and note the deadline is 27 September 2026, so this is already late as strategy and must run now as compliance.

validation_plan.question: Does a full-price European basketball shorts band above EUR 35 exist and clear, and what is the actual unit and price-band distribution by brand and inseam?
validation_plan.method: Purchase syndicated European retail panel coverage for the sports apparel bottoms class - Circana/GfK European panels covering DE, FR, ES, IT, UK - plus negotiated point-of-sale data sharing with KICKZ and Zalando under existing wholesale agreements. Extract two full seasons of basketball shorts units and value by price band, brand and inseam, with full-price versus promotional split. This is the single test the opportunity stands or falls on: if the European market clears between the Decathlon own-brand floor and EUR 20 clearance, EUR 45 has no room and the opportunity is dead on price alone. Note this is NOT a desk read - the marketplace specialist already ran a Europe search and got almost nothing public.
validation_plan.who: Nike EMEA Consumer & Marketplace Insights, with EMEA Key Accounts negotiating the KICKZ/Zalando POS share
validation_plan.cost_time: 8-12 weeks. EUR 120-200k for panel access; POS sharing is a commercial negotiation with no cash cost but real account-relationship cost.

validation_plan.question: Is European basketball participation growing in REGISTRY data, and is the growth in the organised club layer Continental targets or only in casual and spectating?
validation_plan.method: Direct federation registry pull, not media reporting: DBB (Germany), FFBB (France), FEB (Spain), EOK/HEBA (Greece), TBF (Turkey), LKF (Lithuania), KSS (Serbia), Basketball England - licensed players by age band and gender, five-year series, plus Sport England Active Lives for the England weekly-participation series. Explicit test: is EuroLeague's attendance record a spectating story or a playing story? If registrations are flat or falling while attendance rises, this is a fan-apparel opportunity and not a shorts opportunity, and the target consumer must be rewritten. Also resolves whether England's -1% is an outlier or the European pattern, and re-ranks the lead markets on size rather than on which sign of number was findable.
validation_plan.who: Nike EMEA Category Insights, with agency support for federation liaison in Greece, Turkey, Lithuania and Serbia
validation_plan.cost_time: 4-6 weeks. EUR 25-40k with agency support; substantially less if federations respond directly.

validation_plan.question: Does a published claims panel change purchase intent or willingness to pay for a basketball short - and by how much, against which alternative claims?
validation_plan.method: Choice-based conjoint, n=1,200 across Germany, France, Spain and the UK, screened to basketball players and basketball-shorts buyers aged 15-30. Attributes: price (EUR 25/35/45/55), inseam (7in/9in), a published durability figure, a certified UPF figure, a recycled-content figure, pockets, and brand. Deliverable is the utility and willingness-to-pay lift attributable to the claims panel specifically, versus the same short with no panel. This is the only test that can validate the product's reason to exist; run it ONLY if tests 1 and 3 have not already killed the price position, because it is the most expensive item here.
validation_plan.who: Nike Global Consumer Insights with an external conjoint vendor, briefed by EMEA Category Insights

validation_plan.question: Can the wet-state UPF claim actually be tested and published against a named European standard, and does 150gsm recycled double-knit hold a 20-wash dimensional-change and seam-slippage spec at target cost?
validation_plan.method: One materials-lab work order to Nike's Sport Research Lab plus an accredited external textile lab (e.g. Hohenstein or SGS): (a) confirm whether any accredited European method covers UPF at saturation under EN 13758-1/-2 or an equivalent, or whether the wet figure can only be produced under a self-authored protocol - this determines whether the flagship unowned claim is publishable at all; (b) run ISO 6330 at 1/5/10/20 cycles and ISO 13936 seam slippage on the proposed construction; (c) return a landed-cost delta for third-party GRS/RCS certification and the ripstop abrasion panel into the EU, including the EU tariff position no file in this base has modelled. Cheap, fast, and it can kill the differentiator before any consumer money is spent.
validation_plan.who: Nike Sport Research Lab + Global Apparel Materials, with an accredited external textile lab
